abstract: Dr. Calvert discusses the physiology of hormonal contraception, emphasizing the importance of starting low-dose pills on the first day of menses to suppress FSH and prevent follicle formation. He categorizes estrogen into high (50 mcg), low (35 mcg), and very low (15-25 mcg) groups, and progestins into three groups based on progestin and androgen strength. Using a simplified 3x3 matrix, he advises selecting pills by estrogen/progestin profile rather than brand name, and applies this framework to clinical scenarios including acne, dysmenorrhea, breakthrough bleeding, and heavy menstrual bleeding. He also provides practical guidance on managing breakthrough bleeding by timing in the cycle and on tapering high-dose estrogen for acute heavy bleeding.
key_points: Low-dose birth control pills (15-25 mcg ethinyl estradiol) must be started on the first day of menses to suppress FSH and prevent follicle formation; starting even three days late may allow FSH triggering.
Estrogens in pills are ethinyl estradiol and mestranol; mestranol is converted to ethinyl estradiol at a ratio of 50 mcg mestranol to 35 mcg ethinyl estradiol.

Progestins vary by progestin strength and androgenicity: norgestrel/levonorgestrel are strong progestin and strong androgen (acne risk); desogestrel/norgestimate are strong progestin and weak androgen; others are weak progestin and moderate androgen.
Monophasic pills are preferred because they simplify management, only one estrogen and one progestin dose per cycle, avoiding multiple combinations.
For patients with acne, choose a low-androgen progestin (group 2 or 3) and avoid levonorgestrel/norgestrel.
For dysmenorrhea or menorrhagia, select a strong progestin (group 1 or 2) to thin the endometrium and reduce prostaglandins.

Breakthrough bleeding in the first half of the cycle suggests low estrogen or high progestin; management is to increase estrogen or decrease progestin. In the second half, decrease estrogen or increase progestin.
Always recheck blood pressure and assess tolerance at three months after starting pills; do not adjust for spotting earlier as it often resolves.
In women over 40, use low-dose estrogen (group B or C) to minimize hypertension risk; in younger women (15-25), use 35 mcg estrogen for reliability.

For acute heavy bleeding, use high-dose estrogen (50 mcg) three times daily for three days, then taper to twice daily for three days, then once daily; continue pills without withdrawal for 3-6 months to allow anemia recovery.
Smoking plus age over 35 is a contraindication to combined hormonal contraception; patients must stop smoking to use pills.
All combined hormonal contraceptives are equally effective; choose based on side effect profile and patient characteristics, not brand claims.
